claim: LC3 and Atg5 are highly expressed in GFP+ migrating neuroblasts in the RMS.
source: LC3 and Atg5 were highly expressed in GFP+ migrating neuroblasts in the RMS (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing expression of these proteins in neuroblasts.

claim: Between 55 and 60% of neuroblasts are immunolabeled for Atg5 or LC3.
source: Between 55 and 60% of the neuroblasts were immunolabeled for Atg5 or LC3 (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Quantification data from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Less than 10% of astrocytes in the RMS are immunolabeled for autophagy-related proteins.
source: In contrast, less than 10% of astrocytes in the RMS of GFAP-GFP mice were immunolabeled for autophagy-related proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantification data from immunostaining experiments in GFAP-GFP mice shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GFP+-immunolabeled neuroblasts exhibit numerous double-membrane autophagosomes.
source: GFP+-immunolabeled neuroblasts, which were identified based on their typical bipolar morphology with leading and trailing processes, exhibited numerous double-membrane autophagosomes (Figure 1E).
evidence: Electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1E demonstrates the presence of double-membrane autophagosomes.

claim: Western blots of micro-dissected OB and RMS show the presence of autophagosome-associated LC3-II.
source: Western blots of micro-dissected OB and RMS, two regions that contain migrating neuroblasts, showed the presence of autophagosome-associated LC3-II (Figure 1F).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 1F demonstrates LC3-II presence.

claim: A higher proportion of RFP+ vesicles than GFP+/RFP+ vesicles is observed in neuroblasts.
source: We observed a higher proportion of RFP+ than of GFP+/RFP+ vesicles and a highly dynamic bidirectional movement of RFP-LC3 punctae (Figure 1G–I; Video 1).
evidence: Imaging data from RFP-GFP-LC3 fusion protein experiments shown in Figure 1G-I and Video 1.

claim: The migratory phase is associated with 35.5 ± 3.1% GFP+/RFP+ autophagosomes with respect to RFP+ autophagosomes/autolysosomes.
source: The migratory and stationary phases of neuroblasts were associated, respectively, with lower and higher numbers of GFP+/RFP+ autophagosomes with respect to RFP+ autophagosomes/autolysosomes (35.5 ± 3.1% and 44.4 ± 3.1% for the migratory and stationary phases, respectively; p<0.005) (Figure 1K).
evidence: Quantification from time-lapse imaging of RFP-GFP-LC3 in migrating neuroblasts shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The stationary phase is associated with 44.4 ± 3.1% GFP+/RFP+ autophagosomes with respect to RFP+ autophagosomes/autolysosomes.
source: The migratory and stationary phases of neuroblasts were associated, respectively, with lower and higher numbers of GFP+/RFP+ autophagosomes with respect to RFP+ autophagosomes/autolysosomes (35.5 ± 3.1% and 44.4 ± 3.1% for the migratory and stationary phases, respectively; p<0.005) (Figure 1K).
evidence: Quantification from time-lapse imaging of RFP-GFP-LC3 in migrating neuroblasts shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The density of RFP+ punctae is lower during migratory phases (66 ± 6.9%) compared to stationary phases (100 ± 8.8%).
source: Moreover, the density of RFP+ punctae was lower during the migratory phases, whereas the entry of cells into the stationary phase led to a higher density of autophagosomes/autolysosomes (100 ± 8.8% and 66 ± 6.9% for the stationary and migratory phases, respectively; p<0.05) (Figure 1L).
evidence: Quantification from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Bafilomycin reduces the distance of migration of GFP+ neuroblasts from 46.1 ± 2.9 µm to 27.6 ± 3.3 µm.
source: Time-lapse imaging of migrating neuroblasts in acute brain sections revealed that bafilomycin reduces the distance of migration of GFP+ neuroblasts (46.1 ± 2.9 µm for the control vs. 27.6 ± 3.3 µm following the application of bafilomycin, p<0.001, n = 55 and 41 cells from three mice per condition, respectively; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from bafilomycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Bafilomycin decreases the percentage of migratory phases from 53.2 ± 1.6% to 33.8 ± 1.8%.
source: The decrease in migration distance was caused by changes in the percentage of the migratory phases (53.2 ± 1.6% and 33.8 ± 1.8% in the control and bafilomycin-treated cells, respectively, p<0.001, Figure 2E).
evidence: Quantification from time-lapse imaging of bafilomycin-treated cells shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Bafilomycin does not change the speed of migration during migratory phases.
source: There was no change in the speed of migration, which was estimated exclusively during the migratory phases (114.9 ± 5.0 µm/h and 97.6 ± 5.6 µm/h in control and bafilomycin-treated cells, respectively, Figure 2D).
evidence: Speed measurements from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The area of cells occupied by autophagosomes is 75% lower in neuroblasts from Atg5 cKO mice compared to Atg5 WT mice.
source: We first verified the efficiency of autophagy impairment by performing an EM analysis of GFP+ neuroblasts in the RMS of Slc1a3(Glast)CreErt2::Atg5wt/wt::GFP (Atg5 WT) and Atg5 cKO mice and showed that the area of the cells occupied by autophagosomes was 75% lower in the neuroblasts from the Atg5 cKO mice, with no change in the size of individual autophagosomes, indicating that there was a decrease in the total number of autophagosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Electron microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atg5-deficient neuroblasts have a reduced distance of migration (28.5 ± 1.3 µm) compared to control (43.4 ± 1.5 µm).
source: Time-lapse imaging of migrating neuroblasts in acute brain sections from Atg5 WT and Atg5 cKO mice showed that Atg5-deficient neuroblasts have a defect in the distance of migration (43.4 ± 1.5 µm in control mice vs. 28.5 ± 1.3 µm, p<0.001, n = 188 and 198 cells from nine mice per condition for the Atg5 WT and cKO mice, respectively; Figure 2G–H, Video 2).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from Atg5 cKO mice shown in Figure 2G-H and Video 2.

claim: Atg5 deficiency decreases the percentage of migratory phases from 47.8 ± 0.8% to 35.1 ± 0.8%.
source: This decrease was caused by changes in the percentage of the migratory phases (47.8 ± 0.8% in Atg5 WT mice vs. 35.1 ± 0.8% in Atg5 cKO mice, p<0.001), with no change in the speed of migration, which was estimated exclusively during the migratory phases (116.2 ± 2.3 µm/h in Atg5 WT mice vs. 110.4 ± 2.4 µm/h in Atg5 cKO mice; Figure 2G–J).
evidence: Quantification from time-lapse imaging of Atg5 cKO neuroblasts shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: Atg5 deficiency leads to accumulation of neuroblasts in the RMS close to the SVZ (793.3 ± 50.9 cell/mm2) compared to control (594.5 ± 62.9 cell/mm2).
source: An Atg5 deficiency led to the accumulation of neuroblasts in the RMS close to the SVZ (594.5 ± 62.9 cell/mm2 in Atg5 WT mice vs. 793.3 ± 50.9 cell/mm2 in Atg5 cKO mice; p<0.05, n = 7 WT mice and n = 8 cKO mice), with an accompanying decrease in the density of neuroblasts in the rostral RMS (RMS of the OB; noted as RMSOB) (239.2 ± 31.1 cell/mm2 in Atg5 WT mice vs. 171.1 ± 9.7 cell/mm2 in Atg5 cKO mice; p<0.05) and the OB (8.5 ± 1.8 cell/mm2 in Atg5 WT mice vs. 3.8 ± 0.7 cell/mm2 in Atg5 cKO mice, p<0.05) (Figure 2M).
evidence: Cell density quantification from GFP immunostaining shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Atg5fl/fl neuroblasts expressing Cre display the same deficiency in migratory parameters as neuroblasts in Atg5 cKO mice.
source: Atg5fl/fl neuroblasts expressing Cre displayed the same deficiency in migratory parameters as neuroblasts in Atg5 cKO mice (Figure 3B–E and Video 3).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from retroviral Cre expression experiments shown in Figure 3B-E and Video 3.

claim: Neuroblasts from Atg5wt/wt mice infected with either Cre-mNeptune or GFP retroviral particles display normal migration patterns.
source: Importantly, neuroblasts from Atg5wt/wt mice infected either with Cre-mNeptune or GFP retroviral particles or neuroblasts from Atg5fl/fl mice infected with GFP retroviral particles displayed normal migration patterns (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from control retroviral infections shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: There is an 80% decrease in the percentage of neuroblasts expressing Atg12 in Atg12 gRNA-electroporated cells compared to LacZ gRNA-electroporated cells.
source: We observed an 80% decrease in the percentage of neuroblasts expressing Atg12 and electroporated with Atg12 gRNA as compared to LacZ gRNA-electroporated cells (100 ± 0% of Atg12-expressing neuroblasts in LacZ gRNA-electroporated cells and 20.5 ± 2.4% in Atg12 gRNA-electroporated cells, n = 28 cells for LacZ gRNA and n = 43 cells for Atg12 gRNA, three animals per group).
evidence: Immunolabeling quantification data from Atg12 gRNA-electroporated cells.

claim: Atg12 gRNAs reduce the distance of migration from 38.5 ± 3.3 µm to 30.4 ± 2.4 µm.
source: We next performed time-lapse imaging of mCherry+ cells in the RMS 8–13 days post-electroporation and observed that Atg12 gRNAs cause the same defects in cell migration (the distance of migration was 38.5 ± 3.3 µm for LacZ gRNA cells vs. 30.4 ± 2.4 µm for Atg12 gRNA cells, p<0.05, and the percentage of migratory phases was 48.4 ± 1.7% for LacZ gRNA cells vs. 35.5 ± 1.5% for Atg12 gRNA cells, p<0.001) as an Atg5 deficiency (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from Atg12 gRNA electroporation shown in Figure 3H-K.

claim: Atg12 gRNAs decrease the percentage of migratory phases from 48.4 ± 1.7% to 35.5 ± 1.5%.
source: We next performed time-lapse imaging of mCherry+ cells in the RMS 8–13 days post-electroporation and observed that Atg12 gRNAs cause the same defects in cell migration (the distance of migration was 38.5 ± 3.3 µm for LacZ gRNA cells vs. 30.4 ± 2.4 µm for Atg12 gRNA cells, p<0.05, and the percentage of migratory phases was 48.4 ± 1.7% for LacZ gRNA cells vs. 35.5 ± 1.5% for Atg12 gRNA cells, p<0.001) as an Atg5 deficiency (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from Atg12 gRNA electroporation shown in Figure 3H-K.

claim: Atg12 deficiency results in accumulation of cells in the RMS (103.4 ± 17.4%) compared to control (51.5 ± 4.9%).
source: Our analysis revealed an accumulation of Atg12 gRNA-expressing cells in the RMS as compared to LacZ gRNA cells (103.4 ± 17.4% in Atg12 gRNA mice vs. 51.5 ± 4.9% in LacZ gRNA mice, p<0.005), with a decreased cell density in the RMSOB (25.9 ± 5.4% in Atg12 gRNA mice vs. 47.0 ± 6.5% in LacZ gRNA mice; p<0.05) and OB (9.2 ± 1.0% in Atg12 gRNA mice vs. 15.4 ± 1.9% in LacZ gRNA mice; p<0.05, n = 8 and 7 animals for LacZ gRNA- and Atg12 gRNA-electroporated mice, respectively; Figure 3L–M).
evidence: Cell density quantification from Atg12 gRNA-electroporated mice shown in Figure 3L-M.

claim: The ATP/ADP ratio is dynamically regulated during different phases of cell migration.
source: Interestingly, the ATP/ADP ratio was dynamically regulated during the different phases of cell migration (Figure 4B–D) similar to the dynamic changes observed for autophagosomes (Figure 1K–L).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data using PercevalHR biosensor shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Shortly after the beginning of migratory phases, the ATP/ADP ratio starts to decrease, followed by entry into stationary phase and progressive recovery of the ATP/ADP ratio.
source: Shortly after the beginning of the migratory phases, the ATP/ADP ratio started to decrease. This was accompanied by the entry of the cells into the stationary phase and a progressive recovery of the ATP/ADP ratio (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data using PercevalHR biosensor shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: There is a significant difference in ATP/ADP levels during migratory (−0.004 ± 0.001 AU) and stationary phases (−0.001 ± 0.001 AU).
source: This analysis revealed a significant difference in ATP/ADP levels during the migratory and stationary phases of cell migration (−0.001 ± 0.001 AU in the stationary phase vs. −0.004 ± 0.001 AU in the migratory phase, p<0.05, Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantification of ATP/ADP ratio changes shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Changes in the ATP/ADP ratio during different phases of cell migration are not due to changes in intracellular pH.
source: Our time-lapse imaging data suggested that changes in the ATP/ADP ratio during the different phases of cell migration, as determined with the PercevalHR sensor, are not due to changes in the intracellular pH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: pH measurements using pHRed sensor shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ulk1 gRNAs reduce the distance of migration of neuroblasts.
source: We observed a reduced distance of migration for neuroblasts electroporated with Ulk1 or Ulk2 gRNAs (Figure 4F–G) because of reduced migratory phases (Figure 4I), with no any effect on the speed of migration (Figure 4H).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from Ulk1 gRNA electroporation shown in Figure 4F-I.

claim: Ulk2 gRNAs reduce the distance of migration of neuroblasts.
source: We observed a reduced distance of migration for neuroblasts electroporated with Ulk1 or Ulk2 gRNAs (Figure 4F–G) because of reduced migratory phases (Figure 4I), with no any effect on the speed of migration (Figure 4H).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from Ulk2 gRNA electroporation shown in Figure 4F-I.

claim: Compound C (cC) reduces the distance of cell migration due to a decrease in the percentage of migratory phases.
source: cC reduced the distance of cell migration because of a decrease in the percentage of the migratory phases. The speed of migration did not change (Figure 4K–N).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from Compound C treatment shown in Figure 4K-N.

claim: Inhibiting AMPK with cC in Atg5 cKO mice induces no additional changes in the distance of migration or duration of migratory phases.
source: We next inhibited AMPK with cC in acute sections from Atg5 cKO mice and observed no additional changes in the distance of migration or in the duration of the migratory phases (Figure 4K–N).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data from cC treatment in Atg5 cKO mice shown in Figure 4K-N.

claim: Between 24.5 ± 2% and 28.4 ± 1.7% of paxillin-GFP co-localizes in RFP-LC3 vesicles in the cell body and proximal leading process.
source: Our analysis revealed that 24.5 ± 2% to 28.4 ± 1.7% of paxillin-GFP co-localized in RFP-LC3 vesicles in the cell body and the proximal part of the leading process in WT mice, while 42.5 ± 7.9% of paxillin-GFP co-localized in the distal part of the leading process (n = 30 cells from three mice; Figure 5B), suggesting that paxillin is more actively recycled at the leading edge of migrating neuroblasts in the RMS.
evidence: Co-localization analysis from paxillin-GFP and RFP-LC3 co-electroporation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 42.5 ± 7.9% of paxillin-GFP co-localizes in RFP-LC3 vesicles in the distal part of the leading process.
source: Our analysis revealed that 24.5 ± 2% to 28.4 ± 1.7% of paxillin-GFP co-localized in RFP-LC3 vesicles in the cell body and the proximal part of the leading process in WT mice, while 42.5 ± 7.9% of paxillin-GFP co-localized in the distal part of the leading process (n = 30 cells from three mice; Figure 5B), suggesting that paxillin is more actively recycled at the leading edge of migrating neuroblasts in the RMS.
evidence: Co-localization analysis from paxillin-GFP and RFP-LC3 co-electroporation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Atg5 deficiency leads to increased immunolabeling of paxillin in the leading process of neuroblasts, with no changes in the cell soma.
source: We observed that a deficiency in autophagy leads to increased immunolabeling of paxillin in the leading process of neuroblasts, with no changes in the cell soma (n = 38 cells from three mice for Atg5 WT and n = 31 cells from three mice for Atg5 cKO, Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Immunolabeling quantification from Atg5 cKO mice shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Atg12 gRNA electroporation causes paxillin to accumulate in the leading process of neuroblasts compared to control LacZ gRNA-electroporated cells.
source: Immunolabeling for paxillin in brain sections from Atg12 gRNA-electroporated mice revealed that this focal adhesion molecule accumulates in the leading process of neuroblasts compared to control LacZ gRNA-electroporated cells (n = 10 cells from three mice for LacZ gRNA and for Atg12 gRNA, Figure 5E–F).
evidence: Immunolabeling quantification from Atg12 gRNA-electroporated mice shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: BDNF, GABA, GM60001, Y27632, and blebbistatin all induce changes in LC3-II levels.
source: Intriguingly, all these treatments induced changes in LC3-II, the lipidated autophagosomal form of LC3 (Figure 6A and D), suggesting that changes in autophagy are a common signature for neurons displaying either up- or down-regulated migration.
evidence: Western blot data from pharmacological treatments shown in Figure 6A and D.

claim: The level of p62 does not change after pharmacological treatments with BDNF, GABA, GM60001, Y27632, or blebbistatin.
source: Interestingly, while the level of p62 did not change after these pharmacological treatments (Figure 6B), the level of paxillin increased when cell migration decreased and decreased when cell migration increased (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: Western blot data from pharmacological treatments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The level of paxillin increases when cell migration decreases and decreases when cell migration increases.
source: Interestingly, while the level of p62 did not change after these pharmacological treatments (Figure 6B), the level of paxillin increased when cell migration decreased and decreased when cell migration increased (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: Western blot data from pharmacological treatments shown in Figure 6A-E.

claim: Drugs that decrease migration cause an increase in the autophagosome/autolysosome ratio.
source: In line with previous results, drugs that decreased migration caused an increase in the autophagosome/autolysosome ratio, indicating deficient autophagy (Figure 6G).
evidence: Quantification of autophagosome/autolysosome ratio from RFP-GFP-LC3 and Lamp1 immunostaining shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cell migration is a dynamic process composed of migratory phases intercalated with stationary periods.
source: Cell migration is a very dynamic process composed of migratory phases intercalated with stationary periods and is accompanied by structural remodeling, organelle dynamics, and protein trafficking and turnover (Tanaka et al., 2017; Webb et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Tanaka et al., 2017; Webb et al., 2002) to support this statement.

claim: Cell migration entails considerable bioenergetic demand.
source: Cell migration also entails considerable bioenergetic demand, and it is still unclear how migrating cells regulate cellular homeostasis by clearing damaged organelles and aggregated/misfolded proteins, and how the metabolic requirements of neuroblasts are dynamically regulated during the different phases of cell migration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Autophagy is a key evolutionarily conserved intracellular process that controls protein and organelle degradation and recycling.
source: Autophagy is a key evolutionarily conserved intracellular process that controls protein and organelle degradation and recycling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: During autophagy, intracellular materials are sequestered inside double-membrane vesicles (autophagosomes) that then fuse with lysosomes to form autolysosomes.
source: During this process, intracellular materials are sequestered inside double-membrane vesicles (autophagosomes) that then fuse with lysosomes to form autolysosomes in which aggregated/misfolded proteins and damaged organelles are degraded (Yang and Klionsky, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yang and Klionsky, 2010 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy plays an important role in neurodevelopment.
source: Autophagy plays an important role in neurodevelopment (Mizushima and Levine, 2010) and alterations in autophagy have been observed in various human diseases (Yang and Klionsky, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mizushima and Levine, 2010 to support this statement.

claim: Alterations in autophagy have been observed in various human diseases.
source: Autophagy plays an important role in neurodevelopment (Mizushima and Levine, 2010) and alterations in autophagy have been observed in various human diseases (Yang and Klionsky, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yang and Klionsky, 2010 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy is under control of a large protein complex and may be initiated by Ulk1 and Ulk2 proteins.
source: Autophagy is under control of a large protein complex and may be initiated by the Ulk1 and Ulk2 proteins, the downstream effectors of AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) and mTOR (Egan et al., 2011; Petherick et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Egan et al., 2011 and Petherick et al., 2015 to support this statement.

claim: The initiation of autophagy is accompanied by the formation of Atg5–Atg12 complexes and by Atg7-dependent conversion of LC3 from the inactive cytoplasmatic form into the membrane-bound lipidated form (LC3-II).
source: The initiation of autophagy is accompanied by the formation of Atg5–Atg12 complexes and by Atg7-dependent conversion of microtubule-associated protein light chain 3 (LC3) from the inactive cytoplasmatic form into the membrane-bound lipidated form (LC3-II) that is found at the surface of autophagosomes (Simonsen and Tooze, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Simonsen and Tooze, 2009 to support this statement.

claim: A mutation in the Vps15 gene dysregulates endosomal-lysosomal trafficking and autophagy that perturbs neuronal migration.
source: For example, a mutation in the Vps15 gene dysregulates endosomal-lysosomal trafficking and autophagy that, in turn, perturbs neuronal migration (Gstrein et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gstrein et al., 2018 to support this statement.

claim: Ablation of Vps18 leads to neurodegeneration by blocking multiple vesicle transport pathways, including autophagy, and results in abnormal neuronal migration through the upregulation of β1 integrin.
source: Similarly, ablation of Vps18 leads to neurodegeneration by blocking multiple vesicle transport pathways, including autophagy, and results in abnormal neuronal migration through the upregulation of β1 integrin (Peng et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites Peng et al., 2012 to support this statement.

claim: Knock-down of let-7 microRNA decreases the radial migration of neuroblasts by interfering with autophagy.
source: In the OB, knock-down of let-7 microRNA (miRNA) decreases the radial migration of neuroblasts by interfering with autophagy (Petri et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Petri et al., 2017 to support this statement.

claim: Overexpression of beclin-1 or TFEB in neuroblasts lacking let-7 re-activates autophagy and restores radial migration.
source: Overexpression of beclin-1 or TFEB in neuroblasts lacking let-7 re-activates autophagy and restores radial migration (Petri et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Petri et al., 2017 to support this statement.

claim: The ectopic expression of autism-related nonsense Foxp1 mutant-induced autophagy delays radial migration in the developing cortex.
source: On the other hand, the ectopic expression of autism-related nonsense Foxp1 mutant-induced autophagy delays radial migration in the developing cortex (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Li et al., 2019 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy may be triggered by changes in the cellular bioenergetic state.
source: Autophagy may be triggered by changes in the cellular bioenergetic state.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: The regulation of ATP/ADP levels is an important process for cells with high-energy demands such as mature neurons.
source: The regulation of ATP/ADP levels is an important process for cells with high-energy demands such as mature neurons (Hyder et al., 2013; Hill and Colón-Ramos, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hyder et al., 2013 and Hill and Colón-Ramos, 2020 to support this statement.

claim: The modulation of neuronal activity is accompanied by local changes in energy levels and the induction of metabolic compartments near synapses to support synaptic function.
source: The modulation of neuronal activity is accompanied by local changes in energy levels and the induction of metabolic compartments near synapses to support synaptic function (Jang et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Jang et al., 2016 to support this statement.

claim: In both physiological and pathological conditions, neuronal functions may be linked to the activation of the autophagy pathway at the synaptic level where the biogenesis of autophagosomes may take place.
source: In both physiological and pathological conditions, neuronal functions may be linked to the activation of the autophagy pathway at the synaptic level where the biogenesis of autophagosomes may take place (Hill and Colón-Ramos, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hill and Colón-Ramos, 2020 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy and energy consumption act in concert in migrating cells to dynamically regulate the pace and periodicity of the migratory and stationary phases to sustain neuronal migration.
source: Our results show that autophagy and energy consumption act in concert in migrating cells to dynamically regulate the pace and periodicity of the migratory and stationary phases to sustain neuronal migration.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the abstract.

claim: Decreases in ATP levels force cells into the stationary phase and induce autophagy.
source: Time-lapse imaging of autophagosomes and ATP/ADP levels in migrating cells in the rostral migratory stream of mouse revealed that decreases in ATP levels force cells into the stationary phase and induce autophagy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic impairments of autophagy in neuroblasts decreased cell migration due to the longer duration of the stationary phase.
source: Pharmacological or genetic impairments of autophagy in neuroblasts using either bafilomycin, inducible conditional mice, or CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing decreased cell migration due to the longer duration of the stationary phase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Autophagy is modulated in response to migration-promoting and inhibiting molecular cues.
source: Autophagy is modulated in response to migration-promoting and inhibiting molecular cues and is required for the recycling of focal adhesions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Autophagy is required for the recycling of focal adhesions.
source: Autophagy is modulated in response to migration-promoting and inhibiting molecular cues and is required for the recycling of focal adhesions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Neuroblasts born in the SVZ migrate tangentially along the rostral migratory stream (RMS).
source: Neuronal precursors born in the SVZ migrate tangentially along the rostral migratory stream (RMS) and, once in the OB, turn to migrate radially and individually out of the RMS into the bulbar layers (Gengatharan et al., 2016; Kaneko et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gengatharan et al., 2016 and Kaneko et al., 2017 to support this statement.

claim: In the postnatal RMS, neuroblasts travel in chains ensheathed by astrocytic processes along blood vessels.
source: In the postnatal RMS, neuroblasts travel in chains ensheathed by astrocytic processes along blood vessels (Snapyan et al., 2009; Kaneko et al., 2010; Whitman et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Snapyan et al., 2009; Kaneko et al., 2010; and Whitman et al., 2009 to support this statement.

claim: Bafilomycin inhibits the fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes.
source: We stereotactically injected a GFP-encoding retrovirus in the SVZ and analyzed cell migration in the RMS 7–10 days later (Figure 2A). Time-lapse imaging of migrating neuroblasts in acute brain sections revealed that bafilomycin reduces the distance of migration of GFP+ neuroblasts (46.1 ± 2.9 µm for the control vs. 27.6 ± 3.3 µm following the application of bafilomycin, p<0.001, n = 55 and 41 cells from three mice per condition, respectively; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yamamoto et al., 1998 earlier in the text to support this statement about bafilomycin's mechanism.

claim: Paxillin is a focal adhesion protein that is a direct target of LC3-II and is recycled by autophagy during the migration of non-neuronal cells in vitro.
source: Previous studies have shown that paxillin, a focal adhesion protein, is a direct target of LC3-II and is recycled by autophagy during the migration of non-neuronal cells in vitro (Sharifi et al., 2016; Kenific et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Sharifi et al., 2016 and Kenific et al., 2016 to support this statement.

claim: Paxillin is more actively recycled at the leading edge of migrating neuroblasts in the RMS.
source: Our analysis revealed that 24.5 ± 2% to 28.4 ± 1.7% of paxillin-GFP co-localized in RFP-LC3 vesicles in the cell body and the proximal part of the leading process in WT mice, while 42.5 ± 7.9% of paxillin-GFP co-localized in the distal part of the leading process (n = 30 cells from three mice; Figure 5B), suggesting that paxillin is more actively recycled at the leading edge of migrating neuroblasts in the RMS.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher co-localization of paxillin-GFP with RFP-LC3 in the distal leading process.

claim: Several signaling pathways known to affect neuroblast migration converge on autophagy to sustain the pace and periodicity of cell migration through a constant assembly and disassembly of focal adhesions.
source: These results indicate that several signaling pathways known to affect neuroblasts migration converge on autophagy to sustain the pace and periodicity of cell migration through a constant assembly and disassembly of focal adhesions required for cell motility.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple migration-modulating drugs all affect autophagy and paxillin levels.

claim: The efficiency of cell migration and the periodicity of the migratory and stationary phases are directly linked to the energy status of the cells.
source: Tracking intracellular ATP/ADP levels in migrating cells allowed us to demonstrate that the efficiency of cell migration and the periodicity of the migratory and stationary phases are directly linked to the energy status of the cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ATP/ADP tracking experiments in the discussion.

claim: The migratory phase leads to a drop in ATP/ADP levels that is associated with the entry of cells into the stationary phase.
source: The migratory phase led to a drop in ATP/ADP levels that, in turn, was associated with the entry of the cells into the stationary phase.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the ATP/ADP tracking experiments in the discussion.

claim: During the stationary phases, ATP/ADP levels recover due to AMPK activation, following which the cells re-enter the migratory phase.
source: During the stationary phases, ATP/ADP levels recovered due to AMPK activation, following which the cells re-entered the migratory phase.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the ATP/ADP tracking and AMPK inhibition experiments in the discussion.

claim: A decrease in ATP/ADP levels leads to the activation of AMPK, which in turn triggers autophagy.
source: We also showed that a decrease in ATP/ADP levels leads to the activation of AMPK, which in turn triggers autophagy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments in the discussion.

claim: The Ulk1/FIP2000 complex is a key activator of autophagy.
source: One of the downstream targets of AMPK is Ulk1/2 (Egan et al., 2011), and the Ulk1/FIP2000 complex is a key activator of autophagy (Jung et al., 2009; Hara et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites Jung et al., 2009 and Hara et al., 2008 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy regulates cell migration in both the developing and the adult RMS.
source: Our CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in pups and viral vector and transgenic mice approaches in adults demonstrated that autophagy regulates cell migration in both the developing and the adult RMS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments using different age groups in the discussion.

claim: Autophagy is dynamically modulated in migrating cells in the RMS.

claim: Autophagy levels change in response to molecular cues that promote or inhibit migration.

claim: LC3-II directly targets the focal adhesion protein paxillin.
source: These results are in agreement with those of previous in vitro studies showing that LC3-II directly targets the focal adhesion protein paxillin (Sharifi et al., 2016; Kenific et al., 2016).

claim: Decreases in cell migration are linked to a lower recycling rate of paxillin and a higher autophagosome/autolysosome ratio.
source: Indeed, our results suggest that decreases in cell migration are linked to a lower recycling rate of paxillin and a higher autophagosome/autolysosome ratio, while the promotion of cell migration tends to increase paxillin turnover.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments in the discussion.

claim: During cell migration, autophagy inhibits focal adhesion kinase through the Atg13/Ulk1/FIP2000 complex, which promotes cell immobility.
source: During cell migration, autophagy not only recycles focal adhesion proteins but also inhibits focal adhesion kinase through the Atg13/Ulk1/FIP2000 complex, which promotes cell immobility (Caino et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Caino et al., 2013 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy activator protein Vps15 mediates the stability of the cytoskeleton proteins actin and tubulin by decreasing Pak1 activity.
source: Autophagy activator protein Vps15, which is part of Vps34-PI3-kinase complex I, also mediates the stability of the cytoskeleton proteins actin and tubulin by decreasing Pak1 activity (Gstrein et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gstrein et al., 2018 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy is involved in the secretion of matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) and pro-migratory cytokine interleukin-6 (IL6), which promote tumor cell migration.

claim: Autophagy may play a dual role in controlling cell migration by mediating cytoskeleton stability and by mediating the recycling of focal adhesions and the release of pro-migratory factors.
source: These results suggest that autophagy may play a dual role in controlling cell migration. First, it mediates cytoskeleton stability, which maintains the stationary phase, which is required for cellular homeostasis and the regeneration of ATP/ADP levels. Second, it mediates the recycling of focal adhesions and the release of pro-migratory factors, which are required for the entry of cells into the migratory phase.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion synthesizing multiple findings in the discussion.

claim: Cell migration deficit leads to the loss of embryos or functional and cognitive impairments.
source: Cell migration is a crucial mechanism for normal embryonic development, and a cell migration deficit leads to the loss of embryos or functional and cognitive impairments (Ayala et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ayala et al., 2007 to support this statement.

claim: Neuronal migration is preserved in several areas associated with postnatal neurogenesis such as the cerebellum, hippocampus, and subventricular zone (SVZ).
source: Although neuronal migration largely ceases in the postnatal period, it is preserved in several areas associated with postnatal neurogenesis such as the cerebellum, hippocampus, and subventricular zone (SVZ), which is the area associated with the production of neuronal precursors destined for the olfactory bulb (OB).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Energy levels play a role in the coordinated leader-follower cell transition during collective migration of breast cancer cells.
source: Zhang et al. used intracellular measurements of ATP/ADP levels during breast cancer cell invasion to show that energy levels play a role in the coordinated leader-follower cell transition during collective migration (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zhang et al., 2019 to support this statement.

claim: ATP/ADP levels are proportional to the propensity of cancer cells to migrate in vitro.

evidence: The manuscript cites Tuloup-Minguez et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2015 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy promotes cell migration by recycling focal adhesions while the genetic impairment of autophagy leads to decreased cell migration.
source: In contrast, autophagy promotes cell migration by recycling focal adhesions while the genetic impairment of autophagy leads to decreased cell migration (Kenific et al., 2016; Sharifi et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kenific et al., 2016 and Sharifi et al., 2016 to support this statement.

claim: Autophagy depends on the cellular context.
source: As autophagy depends on the cellular context (Klionsky et al., 2012), it is conceivable that differences between these studies can be explained by the types of cells studied and the cellular context in which they were studied.
